Senses.Explanation: Do not let idle learned interpretation bury the mind of the patriarchs — the floating seal that Ming and Qing masters stamp wherever explanation threatens the thing itself: at the close of counsel on the work, over a question left unanswered, before a monk about to speak, and in a letter that quotes the very books it warns against. Dufeng Shan, counselling beginners in a general talk: for one just beginning the work — unless it is language that spurs the work, leave unlooked all the wondrous old-case writings of buddhas and ancestors; the ancients called it seepage: the work never sheets together, and that is not the true cause of the way. Therefore the saying — do not let idle learned interpretation bury the mind of the patriarchs. Nor is it allowed to reckon beneath the root of thought, nor to take the burden up where it is raised, nor to reconcile it as being and nonbeing, nor to weigh it as world-truth and buddha-truth, nor to go searching through writings, idly wasting the years, old and nothing done. Only this is prized: cast off body and world, press close on the bearing phrase you carry, stand on the brink of the ten-thousand-fathom cliff, set foot on the thousand-foot pole — and unaware you step out, turn over, turn a somersault in mid-air, come back laughing aloud; only then may you return and eat this mountain monk's hard staff. Poshan Haiming, showing the assembly: to help people before the fifteenth day — the buddhas protect you; after the fifteenth day — the demons seize you. Right at the fifteenth day — is it the buddha's, or the demon's? Try and say. If you have nothing — do not let idle learned interpretation bury the mind of the patriarchs. Xiaotang, picking old: the courtier annotated the Siyi sutra. The annotating bred false headings in the sutra; the state-teacher's buddha-intent — an arrow tipped upon an arrow. Had there been words besides, he would have pushed over the Chan couch — not only catching that fellow out, but having a way out of his own. And yet — do not let idle learned interpretation bury the mind of the patriarchs. Jiqi Hongchu, in the question-line at the Lingyan temple: the monk was about to press on with words, and the master cut him — do not let idle learned interpretation bury the mind of the patriarchs. Then the verse: no need to open the mouth — weal and life are all from the mind; the bodhisattvas before him help turn the wheel; the great vehicle, deep again deep; cut love and hate, one past and present; the bowl, clay or iron, twice daily in the swing of things — only belly-full and stop. And Fangrong Ruxi, opening the closed retreat: Changsha said — were I to keep hoisting the school's cart, the grass before the hall would grow a fathom deep. Today's robed ones love the stir, hate the quiet, cannot bear it, slip into the packs of fox-spirits, and cannot turn back and look — calling it what principle requires, the spreading of the great way, never knowing they disgrace the school-fires handed down. So the old venerables taught: the intent lies in true working and true waking, not in knowing and talking. The truly awake get the meaning and forget the words, hold command on the adverse and the favoring, win their freedom at the pass of birth and death. Did not the minister Pei ask Huangbo: of four, five hundred in the mountains, how many have the master's way? Huangbo: the way is in the mind's waking — how in speech? Speech only shepherds children. How then does the way wake? Do not let idle learned interpretation bury the mind of the patriarchs. Tianran Hanshi, writing back to the canon-keeper Eryan: the ancients said — do not let idle learned interpretation bury the mind of the patriarchs. This matter most abhors hunting through the pages; among genuine old-craft monks not one jot of that serves. And yet the Records-Mirror also says: there are two who can wither the great tree of the twelvefold chain — one who warms the old and does not forget, one who consults and receives the new. The Song of Awakening too scolds sutras and treatises, while saying itself it woke to the mind-school in the Vimalakirti — are these at odds? And Zuxin, after his waking, told the old Huanglong: the great matter is just so — why does the abbot teach men to watch words and answer words, hunting by the hundred devices?
